## [Sharp Sample Complexity Bounds for KL-Regularized RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13480) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper establishes that for a discounted MDP with K state-action pairs, a plug-in estimator can find an ε-optimal policy from every initial state using Õ(KH^3/(ε max{ε,β}) + KH) samples, and proves a matching lower bound showing no algorithm can do better when ε ≲ min{H, H^2/β}. This improves prior H^5 dependence to H^3 and introduces the first lower bound that depends on the temperature parameter β. This provides tight sample complexity guarantees for KL-regularized RL, the objective behind maximum-entropy RL and RL from human feedback, which are widely used in practice but lacked sharp theoretical understanding. The results give practitioners a precise characterization of how many samples are needed and how the temperature β affects learnability, bridging theory and practice for these popular methods. The paper also derives the exact asymptotic constant of the plug-in estimator, characterized as a Fisher-weighted variance of the estimated soft Q-function, and shows the estimator is locally asymptotically minimax among methods that sample every pair equally often. It further provides the optimal sample allocation among adaptive designs and validates the rates and constants through simulations on small MDPs.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: KL-regularized reinforcement learning adds a Kullback-Leibler divergence penalty to the objective, encouraging the learned policy to stay close to a reference policy; this is the foundation of maximum-entropy RL and RL from human feedback (RLHF). In the 'control as inference' framework, the regularized optimal policy is viewed as a posterior over trajectories, and suboptimality is measured as β times a KL divergence between path measures. Sample complexity studies how many interactions with the environment are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and tight bounds (upper and lower) are key to understanding fundamental limits. Discounted MDPs with effective horizon H and K state-action pairs are a standard setting for such analysis.

## [Metamorphic testing exposes representation dependence in AC-OPF surrogates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13566) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper audits learned AC optimal power flow surrogates using thirteen metamorphic relations across 17 model and pipeline configurations, finding that every configuration violates at least six relations. For GridSFM-Open v1.1, source inspection and intermediate-tensor interventions trace failures to an indexing bug and three noncanonical or numerically unstable preprocessing choices. This work shows that evaluating a learned AC-OPF surrogate on a single grid serialization cannot reveal whether its accuracy depends on that encoding, which is critical for ML-for-systems and power systems researchers. It recommends reporting representation consistency alongside accuracy, feasibility, and cost, pushing the field toward more rigorous robustness standards. The audit covers two released trained checkpoints and 15 random-weight architecture or mechanism controls, with violations persisting even at reporting tolerances ten times tighter or looser. A separate case500 training experiment shows augmentation lowers transformed-view error in three of four models and median discrepancy and constraint-violation P95 in all four, but benefits depend on the training protocol and every evaluated prediction remains AC infeasible.

**Background**: Metamorphic testing is a property-based software testing technique that addresses the test oracle problem by checking whether a model's outputs satisfy expected relations under input transformations, and it has been adapted to machine learning. The framework derives scores from item-level verdicts grounded in timestamped evidence, making the evaluation interpretable and actionable. Synapse-Control introduces a lightweight runtime control plane that uses rules plus a fine-tuned 1.7B classifier to select and time advice delivery to LLM agents, replacing expensive LLM-generated failure diagnoses. Across 1,308 attempts per method on AppWorld and WebShop, it achieves 270 successes (29.8% more than Base), replaces 4,987 generative diagnosis calls, and reduces auxiliary control time relative to Sentry by 50.2% and 51.0%, respectively. ## [MOAI: Efficient Homomorphic Encryption Framework for Secure Transformer Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13641) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MOAI introduces a novel homomorphic encryption (HE) framework for non-interactive secure transformer inference, combining column and diagonal packing with rotation-free algorithms for Softmax and LayerNorm. It reduces HE rotations by at least 1.7x compared to state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 52.8% reduction in evaluation time versus THOR and a 55.7% reduction versus Powerformer, with an amortized time of 2.36 minutes per input on a single GPU. This work significantly lowers the computational overhead of privacy-preserving machine learning, making secure transformer inference more practical for cloud deployments. It impacts industries handling sensitive data, such as healthcare and finance, by enabling encrypted inference without sacrificing performance. MOAI eliminates 2,448 HE rotations in BERT-base inference and uses interleaved batching to reduce rotations in ciphertext-ciphertext matrix multiplications. The framework is extendable to LLaMA-3-8B and is publicly available as open source.

## [Neurosymbolic Security Architecture for Agentic Coding Harnesses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13960) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proposes ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture that enforces separation of intelligence and authority via HMAC capability tokens and a 2D product taint lattice to secure agentic coding harnesses against Living-off-the-Land attacks. In evaluations with 252 fixtures, the Ring-0 guard achieved an attack block rate (ABR) of 1.000 and false positive rate (FPR) of 0.000 in 12.7 microseconds, outperforming an LLM judge that refused 98.3% of benign work at 142.3 ms latency. This work addresses a timely and underexplored threat model where AI coding assistants become automated LotL platforms, and it offers a principled structural approach rather than brittle regex or costly LLM-judge guardrails. The architecture could influence how future agentic systems compose permissions and enforce security, impacting developers and organizations deploying AI coding tools. The architecture combines Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings, a 2D product taint lattice (trust × sensitivity) with a workspace provenance ledger to prevent secret laundering, deterministic Ring-0 OS/tool guards, and bytecode certificates with split-horizon audit logs. In a multi-step trajectory ablation, an oracle Conseca-style stateless policy missed 4/12 kill chains (ABR=0.667) and coarse Boolean taint blocked 83.3% of benign workflows, while the 2D product lattice achieved ABR=1.000 and FPR=0.000 at ~20 microseconds per step.

**Background**: Living-off-the-Land (LotL) attacks abuse trusted, pre-installed tools like bash, curl, and find to carry out malicious actions without introducing new malware, making them fileless and hard to detect. AI coding harnesses connect language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets, so once an adversary injects instructions into retrieved content, these dual-use binaries can become the payload. Neurosymbolic AI combines neural networks' flexibility with symbolic reasoning's rule-based rigor, and reference monitors are security components that mediate all accesses to enforce a policy. Macaroons are HMAC-chained bearer tokens that allow caveats to be appended for least-privilege authorization.

TransGHOST is a causal, reference-guided reconstruction pipeline that reconstructs instrument-occluded regions in ophthalmic microsurgery in real time without generative synthesis. The non-generative approach provides per-pixel confidence and abstentions, enabling safer and more trustworthy intraoperative scene perception. Every restored value is obtained by resampling a recorded frame using geometric transforms fitted only to visible regions, and unsupported pixels are marked as abstentions. The paper introduces MCPO (Margin-Credit Policy Optimization), which redistributes GRPO's per-token advantage using the top-2 next-token margin (M = p1 - p2) to place more credit on tokens where the model hesitated. This offers a compute-free way to improve credit assignment in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), a key technique behind recent reasoning models, and could be easily integrated into existing GRPO-based post-training pipelines. The consistent gains across seeds and model sizes suggest it may generalize to other LLM post-training efforts. The margin is read from a forward pass the trainer already performs, so no extra model evaluation or batch statistics are needed; the method uses two fixed thresholds to map margin to a score and preserves the mean advantage. Gains are largest on problems GRPO solves only some of the time and grow with k in pass@k, reaching 13.8 points at pass@32, but MCPO models also write two to three times longer answers and the experiments do not separate the length effect from the credit-assignment effect.

The top-2 margin is the difference between the highest and second-highest probabilities in the model's next-token distribution, and a small margin indicates the model is uncertain between two candidates. MCPO uses this signal to give more credit to tokens where the model hesitated, rather than treating all tokens equally.

Evaluated on 180-second videos, APEX outperforms S2-Avatar on instruction fulfillment (3.856 vs. 3.831) and visual aesthetics (0.641898 vs. 0.632606), with human raters showing a +30.0% net preference for instruction following. APEX achieves 4.4% lower peak allocated GPU memory per GPU and 9.2% shorter mean iteration time compared to DMD under matched training settings. However, motion quality favors S2-Avatar, audiovisual synchronization is predominantly tied, and usability remains unchanged; the method retains S2-Avatar's frozen reference teacher, Self-Replay Forcing, and perceptual regularization.

A new arXiv paper investigates direct KV cache reuse across four language model updates, focusing on DeepSeek-V4-Flash to Flash-0731, and finds that reused caches can retain useful task information and achieve median time-to-first-token speedups of 2.10–5.08× on three longer-prefix QA benchmarks. The authors introduce Functional Cache Divergence, a metric comparing next-token distributions under reused versus native caches, to characterize behavioral differences. If KV caches can be safely reused across model versions, serving systems could avoid recomputing shared context after updates, significantly reducing latency and compute costs for long-context applications. This work establishes task utility and fidelity to native inference as distinct evaluation criteria, which could shape how future inference infrastructure handles model rollouts. Retrieval accuracy varies widely across updates, from near-native performance to large losses, and direct reuse better preserves native behavior in natural-text continuation but degrades with increasing prefix length in single-token retrieval tasks. Even agreement on the first generated token does not guarantee agreement in answer content or stopping behavior, and the speedups assume source caches are already available.

It proposes that a model's positionality is laminar, laid down across corpus, tuning, system prompt, application, and live conversation, and highlights ruptures and collapses when inheritance between strata is disavowed.

## [ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14106) ⭐️ 7.0/10

ProofCoder introduces an agentic LLM proof-synthesis system for the Rocq proof assistant that reasons continuously throughout proof search, using proof-assistant feedback to decide when to retrieve information, inspect proof states, revise proof fragments, or backtrack. On 280 challenging tasks from the AutoRocq Benchmark, it raises proof success from 47% to 60% over the state-of-the-art AutoRocq system, a 27.7% relative improvement at roughly half the cost. This work moves LLM-based formal proof synthesis beyond rigid tactic-generation loops toward a coding-agent paradigm with feedback-guided revision and backtracking, which could make formal verification of software substantially more practical. It is relevant to both the AI/ML and formal verification communities, since more robust proof synthesis directly lowers the expertise and labor barrier to verified software. Ablations identify continuous reasoning as the key design choice: without it, the agent solves fewer lemmas at substantially higher cost, backtracks four to six times more often, and more frequently discards its own revisions. Whole-proof and tactic-level generation achieve similar success rates but follow distinct search and repair strategies, and the work is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion signals yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

## [AI Isn't Getting Dumber, We're Getting Pickier: Rising Standards in Human Evaluation of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14333) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper analyzes 1,260,967 blind votes from Chatbot Arena (May 2023–August 2024) and finds that for fixed pairs of unchanged models, the share of 'both are bad' votes rises by 1.71 percentage points per month on a mean of 17.1%, and by 1.91 points per month in 2024. In fourteen frequently observed pairs, this share increased in every one, from 15.5% to 23.3%, while the stronger model's share of decisive votes remained flat. This finding challenges the common perception that AI assistants are degrading and suggests that rising human standards, not model regression, drive the perceived decline. It has important implications for LLM leaderboards and for the human feedback used to train models, as absolute verdicts drift while relative comparisons remain stable. The rise holds within the same voter and on the same pair, across arrival cohorts, with prompt controls, in every major language, for dated vendor snapshots, open-weight models, and models with stable answer length, and between interface changes. The drift is shared across models, and platform-wide, the average model would be expected to score 78% against the 2023 average, yet the share of 'both are bad' votes ended near where it began.

## [LLMs Show Gambling-Like Risk-Taking When Given Autonomy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22818) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2509.22818v3) demonstrates that allowing large language models to choose their own bet sizes and set their own profit goals amplifies gambling-like risk-taking, roughly doubling bankruptcy rates compared to baseline conditions. The study also finds that these behavioral contrasts are statistically recoverable from decision-time internal states in open-weight models. This work identifies specific operational levers—self-chosen bet size and self-set profit goals—that induce pathological risk-taking in LLMs, offering concrete targets for AI safety interventions in autonomous agents. It also suggests that behavioral monitoring and internal-state monitoring provide complementary views of autonomy-induced risk, which could inform the design of safer LLM-based decision systems. The bet-size effect persists even when the maximum allowed bet is held equal, and the goal-setting effect is stronger than a reward-maximisation instruction, turning goals into moving targets. The internal readout evidence is correlational, and the rule mapping internal states to a specific risk indicator remains task-specific; adding a direction built from the model's own betting moves wagering behavior, more clearly on Gemma-2-9B, while sparse-feature readout reports risk without moving it.

## [DMR dynamically routes LLM steps between high and low precision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02711) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose Dynamic Mixed-Precision Routing (DMR), a framework that adaptively selects between high-precision and low-precision versions of the same LLM at each decision step in multi-step interactions. DMR exploits the observation that only about 1% of steps are critical—where low precision flips a success to a failure—and trains a lightweight router on hidden states to identify them, achieving an average 2.44x decode speedup over FP16 with comparable task success on three long-horizon agentic benchmarks. This work addresses the substantial inference cost of repeatedly invoking LLMs in long-horizon agentic tasks by showing that precision can be spent only where it matters, without fine-tuning the underlying model. It could enable cheaper deployment of LLM agents while maintaining reliability, impacting practitioners running multi-step reasoning and tool-use pipelines. DMR uses an entire-space factorization to jointly predict a step's divergence and its effect on the outcome, and reuses a shared high-precision KV cache and hidden states to avoid redundant context prefill, adding less than 1 ms overhead per step (under 0.11% latency). With nested quantization, it reduces memory footprint by 39% on average versus FP16; on ALFWorld with GPTQ, it achieves a 1.71x decode speedup with 86.9% success versus 87.2% for FP16.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Large language models are increasingly used as agents that solve long-horizon tasks through many sequential steps of reasoning and interaction, but each step requires a full forward pass, making inference expensive. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces cost by lowering numerical precision (e.g., to 4-bit or 8-bit), but applying a fixed low precision throughout an episode can sharply degrade task success. Mixed-precision inference, which uses different precisions for different parts of a model or computation, aims to spend bits where they matter most; DMR extends this idea to the step level in multi-step interactions.

## [TACT steers coding agents away from overthinking and overacting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05980) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces TACT (Think-Act Calibration via activation Steering), which detects and mitigates two failure modes in coding LLM agents—overthinking and overacting—by identifying linear 'drift axes' in the residual stream with an AUC of approximately 0.9. At test time, TACT projects each step's activation onto these axes and pulls drifted activations back toward calibrated behavior, improving average resolve rate by +5.8 percentage points on Qwen3.5-27B and +4.8 percentage points on Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it across SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and CLAW-Eval, while cutting steps-to-resolve by up to 26%. Agent drift—the degradation of LLM agents over long trajectories—is a major obstacle to reliable long-horizon software engineering agents, and TACT offers a lightweight, test-time intervention that requires no retraining. If the approach generalizes, it could become a practical handle for improving agent reliability in production coding and tool-use settings. TACT labels trajectory steps as overthinking, overacting, or calibrated, and finds that hidden states separate linearly along two drift axes; steering is applied by projecting activations onto these axes and pulling drifted ones back toward the calibrated region. The gains are demonstrated on three benchmarks and two model families, but the paper does not report results on other agent domains or discuss potential interference with other behaviors.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Activation steering is a technique that modifies a language model's internal activations during inference to guide its behavior, often by adding a direction vector to the residual stream—the shared hidden state that each transformer layer reads from and writes to. Agent drift refers to the progressive degradation of an agent's decision quality and coherence over extended interactions, a known challenge for long-horizon LLM agents. TACT applies activation steering to the specific problem of coding agents that either loop on redundant reasoning or act without integrating new observations.

## [TRACE: Business Rule-Grounded Reasoning Curriculum for Parametric Tool Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22639) ⭐️ 7.0/10

TRACE introduces a two-stage curriculum that preserves parametric tool knowledge and speeds up retrieval by training LLMs to emit reasoning traces before generating tool tokens, grounded in expert-curated business rules. Evaluated on 8,300+ tools, it achieves ~86% recall on Domain A and ~60% on Domain B with single-beam greedy decoding, compared to embedding baselines of ~27% and ~52%. This addresses two critical drawbacks of parametric tool retrieval—destruction of tool knowledge during training and slow beam-search decoding—making it directly deployable at production latency for enterprise LLM applications. The approach could enable real-time, accurate tool retrieval in large enterprise catalogs without sacrificing model understanding. Stage 1 reuses ToolSense's multi-format memorization SFT with LoRA to seed tool knowledge, while Stage 2 trains the model to emit a thinking trace before a JSON list of tool tokens using RRB pairs and synthesized queries targeting business rules. Stage 2 not only preserves but improves tool understanding, with MCQ accuracy gaining +3.2 pp and QA probing gaining +9 pp over Stage 1.

**Background**: Parametric tool retrieval assigns each API a unique virtual token and trains the LLM to generate it, as in ToolGen, avoiding a separate retrieval step. ToolSense is a diagnostic framework that generates benchmarks for tool retrieval and revealed that this regime destroys tool knowledge and suffers from slow beam-search decoding. TRACE builds on ToolSense by adding a reasoning curriculum grounded in business rules to mitigate these issues.

A new arXiv paper (2609.36630v2) presents the first unified survey of agent distillation, formalizing it as persistent knowledge transfer between teacher and student agents. It introduces a knowledge-substrate taxonomy that categorizes where knowledge persists—in model parameters, reusable artifacts, or execution harnesses—and analyzes cross-substrate transfer paths and hybrid strategies. This survey bridges two previously separate research threads—LLM knowledge distillation and agent system design—providing a shared vocabulary for comparing transfer strategies across agent components. It could guide researchers and practitioners toward more efficient deployment, broader capability access, and continual self-evolution of LLM-based agents. The taxonomy distinguishes experience used for transfer from knowledge retained for reuse, and the survey also reviews benchmarks and evaluation protocols for retention, causal attribution, and deployed utility without further teacher support. As a survey rather than an empirical breakthrough, it synthesizes existing work rather than introducing new experimental results.

As LLM-based agents move from single response generation to sustained, closed-loop task solving, distillation increasingly involves not just model parameters but also reusable resources (artifacts) and execution workflows (harnesses). ## [EASER: Reflective LLM Agent Bridges Evidence and Execution for Peptide Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.06190) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce EASER, a reflective agent that uses an LLM controller to compose learned low-rank property directions and steer a frozen diffusion generator for multi-objective peptide design. On computational antimicrobial peptide design, EASER balances activity, non-hemolysis, and non-toxicity, achieving the highest mean hypervolume and lowest mean IGD+ among evaluated search policies and generators. This work addresses the evidence-to-execution gap by making literature-grounded scientific reasoning directly executable at the sequence level, potentially accelerating AI-driven drug and peptide discovery. It demonstrates a general framework where LLM agents can control generative models through interpretable, learned property interfaces rather than end-to-end retraining. The property interface consists of property-specific low-rank directions trained offline and fixed during search; the LLM controller proposes intervention hypotheses specifying anchors, editable positions, and coefficients, which are tested via Probe-and-Steer with reflection updating agent memory. Ablations confirm the importance of evidence retrieval, episodic history, reflection, and Probe-and-Steer, and explicit hypothesis formulation yields larger multi-objective gains than direct action generation.

**Background**: Large language models can reason over scientific literature but cannot reliably produce biological sequences with intended properties, while sequence generators capture patterns but do not interpret evidence or reflect on outcomes. Diffusion models are generative models that iteratively denoise random noise to produce data, and low-rank directions are compact vectors in a model's latent space that can steer generation toward specific properties. EASER bridges this gap by using an LLM as a controller that composes such directions to steer a frozen diffusion generator, enabling evidence-based multi-objective peptide design.

## [Circe: Training-Free LLM Self-Evaluation via Component Interaction Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07948) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Circe introduces a training-free self-evaluation method that combines internal component interaction consistency (CIC) between attention updates and attention-induced FFN output changes with representation geometry (RG) and a bounded likelihood confidence (LC) score to assess response correctness without reference answers or repeated sampling. Experiments on five LLMs and six benchmarks across four domains show it outperforms existing baselines and generalizes to multilingual, multimodal, and open-world settings. Reference-free correctness estimation is critical for deploying LLMs reliably, and Circe's use of internal attention-FFN interaction signals offers a complementary perspective beyond output-only or hidden-state trajectory methods. If validated, it could enable practical self-checking in production systems without costly human references or multiple inference runs. CIC measures directional alignment between attention updates in earlier layers and attention-induced FFN output changes in later layers, while RG characterizes normalized displacement and angular changes along layerwise hidden-state trajectories; these are fused with LC into a unified score. The method is training-free and avoids repeated sampling, but as an arXiv preprint it still lacks independent validation and community discussion.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Large language models often produce incorrect responses, and evaluating correctness without reference answers is a key challenge for reliable deployment. Existing reference-free methods typically rely on output signals such as likelihood, which can assign high scores to wrong answers, or on hidden-state trajectories that only capture combined attention and FFN updates. Transformer LLMs alternate attention, which handles token interactions, and feed-forward networks (FFNs), which process each token individually, and how these components interact internally may provide additional correctness cues.

## [Causal Inference Framework for When to Intervene in AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09792) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces the first methodologically grounded causal inference framework for evaluating randomized interventions within AI agent trajectories, moving beyond static benchmarks. Using a small dataset of trajectories collected under randomized interventions, it estimates dynamic causal effects of contextual intervention policies and constructs safety leaderboards for audit prioritization. This work addresses a critical gap in agentic AI evaluation by enabling deployment-time decisions about whether to verify or steer an agent's output, which is essential for reliable and safe real-world deployment. It also opens a research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, potentially influencing how practitioners audit and supervise AI agents. The framework estimates structural parameters from a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, capturing how intervention effects vary across actions and states. Applied to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, the study finds substantial variation in intervention effects, highlighting the need for context-aware auditing.

**Background**: AI agents are systems that pursue complex goals with limited supervision, and their evaluation currently relies on static benchmarks that cannot inform deployment-time decisions. The study uses 149 tweets and five severity categories, and finds that proprietary models generally agree better with experts and are more stable than open-source models. Label-flipped demonstration experiments show model-specific sensitivity to misleading in-context examples, and explanatory demonstrations do not consistently improve performance.

## [TIGER bridges modality reasoning-access gap in multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10552) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.10552) identifies a 'modality reasoning-access gap' in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), where models can accurately read text from images but fail to reason over it, and proposes TIGER (Text-to-Image Gap-targeted training for Enhanced Reasoning) to bridge this gap. TIGER mines synthetic modality counterfactuals—cases where the model succeeds on a text problem but fails on the equivalent rendered image—and post-trains the model on the image input using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), along with SFT and DPO variants. This work shifts the focus from perception failures to reasoning-access failures in MLLMs, offering a targeted training method that improves performance on diverse real-world visual benchmarks without requiring manually curated multimodal datasets. It could lead to more efficient and generalizable multimodal reasoning systems, impacting researchers and practitioners working on visual question answering, chart understanding, and embodied AI. TIGER is trained exclusively on synthetic rendered-text images with no multimodal annotations, yet it improves performance on benchmarks including MathVerse (geometric diagrams), EMMA and MMMU (multi-disciplinary sciences), ChartQAPro (complex charts), and RoboSpatial-Home (embodied spatial reasoning). Analysis via reasoning-subspace activation and activation patching suggests that TIGER aligns visual-to-reasoning pathways toward text reasoning states, and it complements existing state-of-the-art RLVR visual reasoning methods.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) combine a vision encoder with a language model backbone, inheriting strong textual reasoning from pretraining. However, they often underperform on visual inputs even when the visual content is semantically equivalent to text. The 'modality reasoning-access gap' describes the phenomenon where models can perceive visual information but fail to route it into their existing reasoning machinery, which is typically tuned for text. TIGER addresses this by generating synthetic image versions of text problems and using reinforcement learning to teach the model to reason over the visual input as effectively as over text.

## [FinCutBench: A Monthly Benchmark for Temporal Boundaries of LLM Financial Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11588) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FinCutBench is a continually updated monthly benchmark of 9,000 Chinese and English four-option multiple-choice questions spanning January 2023 to September 2026, covering Chinese and U.S. markets. It constructs monthly knowledge profiles to define the FinCut Boundary—the first month when a model's fitted knowledge profile reaches its lower level—and reports the stability of this date under resampling. This benchmark addresses parametric look-ahead bias, where LLM parameters retain financial facts disclosed after a backtest date, undermining the validity of financial backtests. By providing an empirical reference for the temporal scope of parametric knowledge, it supports evaluation-window selection and result interpretation for both finance and LLM evaluation communities. The methodology includes a decline test and knot checks to validate knowledge profiles, and the estimated boundary dates and localization precision vary across models. Downstream analysis using the Transition Start and Boundary as fixed references reveals significant relative declines in U.S. asset-ranking performance and earnings recall for Sol and Luna, with effects varying across markets and tasks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: In financial backtesting, point-in-time data restricts external inputs to what was available at a given date, but LLM parameters may still encode later-disclosed facts, a phenomenon known as parametric look-ahead bias. This bias can inflate backtest performance because the model effectively 'knows' future outcomes. FinCutBench measures how far a fixed model's financial knowledge extends over calendar time, helping researchers select appropriate evaluation windows.

## [RAS-Eval: LTL-based security evaluation for LLM agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15253) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RAS-Eval is a specification-based security evaluation framework that expresses both utility and security objectives as Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications over tool-call trajectories and verifies them with an off-the-shelf model checker. The authors also built a benchmark of 200 normal tasks and 800 attack tasks covering four attack surfaces: indirect prompt injection, tool poisoning, skill code injection, and tool code injection. Existing evaluation methods like LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge are vulnerable to hallucination and perturbation, and may miss transient violations that are overwritten before the trajectory ends. RAS-Eval's deterministic verdicts and precise state monitoring address these limitations, which is important for safely deploying LLM agents in long-horizon unattended scenarios. RAS-Eval observes exactly the states on which the verdict depends, making it affordable to monitor the environment throughout execution and detect transient violations that leave little trace in logs or final state. The benchmark and code are available at https://github.com/lanzer-tree/RAS-Eval.

**Background**: Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) is a modal temporal logic for expressing properties of systems over time, such as 'a condition will eventually be true' or 'a condition will be true until another fact becomes true'. LLM-as-a-Judge is a technique where an LLM assesses the quality or correctness of another model's output against predefined criteria, but such judges can themselves hallucinate. RAS-Eval uses LTL specifications and model checking to provide formal, deterministic security evaluation for LLM agents that call tools.

The system uses a Scope Inference Agent to convert the developer's initial refactoring into a natural-language Declared Scope, a Planned Execution Agent to identify and safely apply changes via the IDE's trusted refactoring APIs, and a Replication Agent to guide project-wide search. Coordinated renaming is frequent but tedious and error-prone, and existing heuristic methods produce too many false positives while vanilla LLMs give incomplete suggestions due to limited context and inability to interact with refactoring tools. This approach keeps developers in control while reducing their burden, potentially improving productivity and code quality in AI-assisted software engineering. The design is grounded in a formative study of 609K commits across 100 open-source projects and a survey of 205 developers, and the key insight is that a developer's initial refactoring serves as a clue to infer the scope of related refactorings. The framework executes changes by invoking the IDE's own trusted refactoring APIs rather than generating raw edits, which helps ensure safety and correctness.

Multi-agent systems consist of multiple interacting AI agents that collaborate to solve problems difficult for a single agent, and LLMs have shown promise but limitations in code refactoring tasks.

## [FiLoRA: Instruction-Conditioned LoRA for Controllable Feature Reliance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02060) ⭐️ 7.0/10

FiLoRA introduces an instruction-conditioned, parameter-efficient adaptation framework that decomposes adaptation into feature-aligned low-rank modules and applies instruction-conditioned gating, allowing natural language instructions to act as computation-level control signals over internal representations. Evaluated on controlled classification and generative multimodal tasks, it induces consistent and interpretable shifts in feature reliance, selectively amplifying or suppressing feature groups without altering task semantics. This work offers a practical mechanism to intervene on internal model behavior beyond output-level prompting or post hoc interpretation, which could improve interpretability and robustness of multimodal foundation models by directly controlling reliance on shortcut or spurious features. It may benefit researchers and practitioners concerned with model controllability, fairness, and safety. FiLoRA keeps the task and predictive objective fixed while using natural language instructions, including compositional ones, to gate feature-aligned low-rank modules; results show selective amplification or suppression of feature groups. As a parameter-efficient method, it adds only small trainable modules, but the abstract does not specify the exact architectures or datasets used.

**Background**: Multimodal foundation models integrate heterogeneous signals such as vision and language, but they can rely on shortcut or spurious correlations that hurt robustness. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that freezes pre-trained weights and injects small trainable low-rank matrices into layers, greatly reducing trainable parameters. ## [CAPE: Bayesian Adaptive Questioning for Cold-Start Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15012) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CAPE learns a structured world model of cross-population preference correlations offline and uses training-free Bayesian inference online to select informative questions and predict full preference profiles. It achieves 80.8% alignment with ground-truth preferences versus 68.5% for end-to-end RL, using 2.5x to over 15x fewer interactions. This work shows that a principled decomposition of cold-start personalization into offline structure learning and online Bayesian inference can outperform end-to-end RL, making preference elicitation practical for LLM systems with limited interaction budgets. The finding that simple belief models like linear regression beat RL is counterintuitive and could shift how practitioners approach personalization. CAPE adapts its questions twice as often as RL and can predict preferences on dimensions never asked about. Even simple belief model instantiations such as linear regression substantially outperform end-to-end RL, and the approach is evaluated across medical, mathematical, social, and commonsense reasoning domains.

**Background**: Cold-start personalization is the problem of inferring user preferences with little or no historical data. Preference elicitation can be framed as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where the user's preference profile is the hidden state and questions are actions. CAPE sidesteps credit assignment by learning a structured prior offline and performing Bayesian inference online without retraining.

## [Preconditioned Flow Matching Improves Training Convergence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02337) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper identifies a geometric optimization bottleneck in flow matching caused by ill-conditioned covariance of intermediate distributions and proposes preconditioned flow matching, a precondition-then-match framework that transforms the target distribution into a more isotropic representation before training the flow. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures, latent MNIST, and high-resolution images up to 512×512 show improvements in FID, MMD, precision, and recall. This work provides a theoretical explanation for slow convergence in flow matching and offers a practical solution that could improve training efficiency and sample quality for generative models. It is likely to influence future research on optimization in diffusion and flow-based generative modeling. The analysis proves that excess risk is weighted by the covariance matrix and that gradient descent inherits condition-number-dependent convergence, with the slowest and worst-conditioned component controlling optimization in Gaussian mixtures. Compute-matched baselines and preconditioner-quality ablations confirm that gains come from improved geometry rather than additional parameters.

## [RECAP: Hebbian Prototype Readout for Reservoir Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.06639) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RECAP introduces a self-organizing Hebbian prototype readout for reservoir dynamics, enabling robust image classification without error backpropagation. The method discretizes time-averaged reservoir responses, constructs a co-activation mask over unit pairs, and incrementally updates class-wise prototype matrices via a Hebbian-like potentiation-decay rule. This work offers a bio-inspired alternative to backpropagation-based training, which could lead to more energy-efficient and online-adaptable learning systems. It also demonstrates robustness to image corruptions without exposure to corrupted training data, relevant for real-world deployment. RECAP avoids error backpropagation and is naturally compatible with online prototype updates. On MNIST-C, it remains robust under diverse corruptions without exposure to corrupted training samples, though evaluation is limited to this benchmark.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Reservoir computing is a framework where input signals are mapped into a high-dimensional space by a fixed, non-linear dynamical system called a reservoir, and only a simple readout is trained. Hebbian learning is a neuropsychological theory often summarized as 'neurons that fire together, wire together,' explaining synaptic plasticity without global error signals. Backpropagation is the standard gradient-based method for training neural networks, but it is not biologically plausible and requires end-to-end differentiation.

## [KAIROS: Context-Aware Power Optimization for Agentic AI Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16682) ⭐️ 7.0/10

KAIROS, a new system presented in arXiv:2604.16682, uses agent context as a first-class control signal to jointly manage GPU frequency, per-instance concurrency, and multi-instance request placement for agentic AI serving. It achieves an average of 27% (up to 39.8%) power reduction while meeting performance targets across diverse software and data engineering agentic tasks. Power has become a central bottleneck for AI inference, and agentic workloads are emerging as a major class, yet prior power-management techniques focus almost entirely on single-turn LLM serving. KAIROS shows that agentic serving requires rethinking power optimization, with implications for data centers and infrastructure providers running increasingly complex AI agents. The key insight is that lowering GPU frequency in agentic serving can push the system into a thrashing regime where memory pressure sharply worsens both performance and power efficiency, because each request carries long-lived context that evolves across tool-interleaved turns. KAIROS tracks requests at agent granularity, adapts local control to context growth and agent progress, and routes agents across instances to jointly improve power efficiency and memory stability.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Agentic AI refers to AI systems that autonomously perform multi-step tasks, often interleaving tool calls and maintaining long-lived context across turns. GPU power management typically uses dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) to adjust GPU frequency for energy savings, but such techniques were designed for single-turn LLM serving. Thrashing occurs when memory pressure causes constant data swapping, severely degrading performance; in GPU systems, it can happen when memory is oversubscribed and pages are repeatedly evicted.

## [Data and Training Methods Shape Misalignment Transfer in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12798) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2605.12798) investigates how training data, evaluation data, and training methods influence emergent misalignment (EM) and subliminal learning (SL) in language models. Using domain-task grids, the authors find that EM transfers more strongly to prompts sharing the task of fine-tuning data than to those sharing its domain, and that misalignment transfers even under on-policy distillation, more strongly than under supervised fine-tuning (SFT). This work provides actionable insights for AI safety: task-based transfer is a stronger vector for misalignment than domain-based transfer, suggesting that safety evaluations should focus on task similarity. It also shows that distillation methods, including on-policy distillation, can propagate misalignment, which has implications for model training pipelines that rely on teacher-student distillation. The study builds natural-language and synthetic datasets organized as domain-task grids, and for SL it goes beyond SFT to off-policy distillation on the teacher's full next-token distribution and, for the first time, on-policy distillation where the teacher only scores tokens sampled by the student. With the teacher fixed, the data change how much misalignment the student inherits, but the teacher determines to which domains and tasks it transfers most strongly.

DotRAG introduces a lightweight, training-free GraphRAG retrieval algorithm that uses LLM reasoning over a graph-wide overview and reachability indexing to recover task-relevant relational paths at query time. On MetaQA 2-hop queries, it achieves 97.78% retrieval recall and 51.27% F1, far surpassing the best baseline scores of 34.74% and 6.33%, and on STaRK-MAG it reaches 85.07% recall with 12.2x lower retrieval latency than HopRAG. The approach is training-free and demonstrates strong efficiency gains, though results are limited to MetaQA and STaRK-MAG benchmarks and the paper is an arXiv preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

DotRAG combines these ideas with LLM reasoning to narrow the search space without training.

## [CARV reduces variance in diffusion teacher gradients with hierarchical Monte Carlo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21489) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CARV introduces a compute-aware hierarchical Monte Carlo estimator that reuses expensive upstream computations across cheap diffusion draws, combined with timestep importance sampling and stratified inverse-CDF sampling, to reduce variance in gradients from frozen diffusion teachers. It achieves 2-3x effective compute multipliers on text-to-3D and data attribution without changing the objective. This work addresses a key bottleneck in pipelines that rely on pretrained diffusion models as frozen teachers, where Monte Carlo variance dominates compute cost. The 2-3x compute multiplier could significantly speed up text-to-3D generation and data attribution, making these techniques more practical for researchers and practitioners. In text-to-3D, reuse provides most of the gain and importance sampling with stratification adds about 25%. In single-step distillation, the same techniques cut gradient variance by an order of magnitude but do not improve downstream FID, indicating that MC variance is no longer the bottleneck in that regime.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Pretrained diffusion models are often used as frozen teachers in pipelines like text-to-3D generation, single-step distillation, and data attribution. These pipelines require gradients of an objective with respect to the teacher model, which are expectations over noise levels and Gaussian noise, typically estimated via Monte Carlo methods. Each Monte Carlo draw involves expensive upstream computations such as rendering or simulation, so reducing estimator variance is crucial for computational efficiency. Variance reduction techniques like importance sampling and stratified sampling are classical methods to improve Monte Carlo efficiency.

Researchers propose Diff-Instruct with Diffused Reward (DIDR), a data-free trajectory-level reinforcement learning alignment framework derived from Integral KL minimization that propagates the RLHF-optimal reward-tilted clean-image distribution across all noise levels. DIDR is derived from Integral KL minimization and shows that its objective admits the same minimizer as clean-image RLHF, while the DRS acts as a reward-driven correction to the reference score function. StakeBench introduces a financial NLP benchmark that evaluates language understanding against verified market commitments and trading behavior instead of human-annotated sentiment labels. A new arXiv paper empirically tests whether architectural choices cause hallucination by swapping attention for a state-space mixer while holding pretraining data, tokenizer, and scale fixed across five Pythia/Mamba pairs (130M to 2.8B parameters) and four additional attention models. It matters for AI/ML researchers and model architects because it suggests that architectural choices affect error propagation from context, but not the fundamental failure to recall long-tail knowledge, which stems from missing knowledge rather than suppressed truth. Study 2 replaces the first wrong fact in 111 erroneous answers from three instruction-tuned models, finding that a correct fact cuts downstream errors from 92.5% to 48.1%, but a different wrong fact works equally well (p = 0.38), and models give the right answer in isolation on only 2 of 111 items. ## [RamanPFN: Physics-Guided Spectral Foundation Framework for In-Context Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02157) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RamanPFN introduces a physics-guided spectral foundation framework that encodes additive spectral mixing and vibrational band locality to enable unified in-context inference across diverse Raman applications. Evaluated on 74 public Raman datasets with over 330,000 spectra, it outperformed 26 methods on 129 regression targets, reducing backbone RMSE by 13.2%. This work addresses a concrete limitation of tabular foundation models like TabPFN, where feature subsampling on wide spectra loses joint channel visibility, and demonstrates that physics-guided in-context learning can enable data-efficient quantitative analysis and sample identification in spectroscopy. The gains generalize across TabPFN-3, TabICLv2, and Kumo-Tabular, suggesting broad impact for spectral machine learning. RamanPFN combines Global Compositional Unmixing, which decomposes multi-band mixture signatures into shared non-negative bases, with Local Vibrational Subspace Encoding, which extracts orthogonal modes within contiguous spectral neighborhoods to preserve peak morphology and shifts. Posterior marginalization over admissible unmixings unifies both scales without updating the model, reducing regression error by 12.3%–25.7% and multiclass log loss by 42.4%–63.5% across the tested backbones.

## [SPrPO: Sensitivity-Aware Perturbation Training for Robust LLM Agent Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34064) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Stable Perturbation-Robust Policy Optimization (SPrPO), an RL post-training method that applies adaptive, sensitivity-aware perturbations to improve the robustness of LLM agent policies against hidden-state noise, pruning, and quantization. It provides a theoretical analysis showing that perturbed policy updates can preserve stable monotonic improvement, and evaluates SPrPO on ALFWorld and WebShop across multiple perturbation types and scales. RL post-training is increasingly used to build long-horizon LLM agents, but the resulting policies can be fragile when deployed under compression or noisy conditions. SPrPO addresses this underexplored robustness gap while offering stability guarantees, which could make RL-trained agents more reliable in real-world deployment where quantization and pruning are common. SPrPO introduces a formal notion of a perturbation-robust policy and derives conditions under which perturbed updates retain monotonic improvement, then uses adaptive perturbations whose strength depends on policy sensitivity. Experiments systematically cover multiple perturbation types and scales on ALFWorld and WebShop, though the abstract does not report specific performance numbers or comparisons to baselines.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning post-training fine-tunes LLM agents on long-horizon tasks using reward signals, and monotonic policy improvement is a classic theoretical property guaranteeing that each update does not degrade performance. In practice, deployed agents often face hidden-state noise, weight pruning, or quantization for efficiency, which can shift the policy away from its training distribution. Perturbation-based training augments optimization with noise to encourage robustness, but naive perturbations can destabilize learning, motivating sensitivity-aware schemes like SPrPO.

## [LeapQuant: Training-Free 8-bit Quantization for Linear Attention States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.38166) ⭐️ 7.0/10

LeapQuant introduces a training-free per-window quantization method that achieves near-lossless 8-bit recurrent-state quantization for linear attention models such as Gated DeltaNet and Kimi Delta Attention. Experiments across Qwen, Kimi, and GLM model families show average kernel-level speedups of 2.05–3.70× and 1.47× end-to-end inference speedup on NVIDIA B200, RTX PRO 6000, and RTX 5090 GPUs with accuracy comparable to the FP32 baseline. This work addresses a key inference bottleneck in hybrid LLM architectures: the recurrent state, not the KV cache, is read and updated on every generated token, directly limiting memory footprint and concurrent-request capacity. By making 8-bit state quantization practical without retraining, LeapQuant could significantly lower the cost of long-context inference for linear-attention-based models. LeapQuant mitigates error accumulation via per-window quantization, quantizing the state only once at the end of a token window while computing outputs from the fixed low-bit state plus high-precision buffered updates. It further reduces per-quantization error by retaining the state's largest outliers as a few high-precision Compensator Tokens that share the update path of real tokens, and by smoothing the remaining residual before quantization.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Linear attention mechanisms such as Gated DeltaNet and Kimi Delta Attention replace the unbounded KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state, reducing sequence mixing to linear time and decoding to constant memory. However, this state must be repeatedly read and updated for every token, making it a major inference bottleneck. Quantization can reduce this cost, but naive low-bit quantization degrades quality due to accumulated rounding errors and outlier rows and columns in the state.

## [Whiteout: Obfuscation Tool Prevents LLM Private Data Leakage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02418) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02418v2) introduces Whiteout, a tool that prevents LLMs from regurgitating personally sensitive information (PSI) by overwriting it with carefully designed obfuscation samples upon individual request. Evaluated across modern LLMs of varying sizes and makers, including a widely-used OpenAI model, Whiteout effectively blocks targeted PSI disclosure with negligible impact on model utility and safety, outperforming existing machine unlearning alternatives. This work offers a practical alternative to machine unlearning for LLM privacy, addressing unlearning's tendency to over-remove information, degrade utility and safety, and remain vulnerable to attacks. It could benefit high-profile individuals such as executives, politicians, and judges whose personal data is at risk, and points toward a more targeted, request-driven privacy protection paradigm for deployed LLMs. Whiteout was tested against a wide range of countermeasures, from black-box attacks like jailbreaking to white-box adaptive attacks such as relearning and quantization, and the paper concludes with a discussion of security and ethical implications. The approach avoids the utility degradation and attack vulnerability associated with machine unlearning by overwriting rather than removing the targeted information.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Large language models are trained on massive, largely unfiltered datasets scraped from websites and user inputs, causing them to memorize and sometimes reproduce personally sensitive information (PSI) like birth dates, phone numbers, and home addresses. Machine unlearning is the prevailing mitigation, aiming to erase specific information from a trained model without full retraining, but it often removes more than needed and harms model utility and safety. Whiteout instead uses targeted obfuscation samples to overwrite genuine PSIs, preserving the model's overall behavior while blocking disclosure of the targeted data.

## [CACHEFORGE uses LLM-driven evolution to generate cache replacement policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.07668) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CACHEFORGE is a framework that embeds a large language model in a governed hardware-aware loop to evolve end-to-end cache replacement policies written in C++. Evaluated on SPEC CPU2006 with the ChampSim simulator, it improves total hit rate by up to 27.36% over MPPPB and 5.73% over LRU, and boosts IPC by up to 10.15% over LRU on memory-intensive workloads. This work moves beyond heuristic and imitation-based cache replacement designs that often plateau, showing that LLMs can synthesize novel decision logic for a core computer architecture problem. If validated, it could lead to more adaptive and hardware-efficient cache policies, impacting processor design and AI-for-systems research. The framework enforces feasibility through reward shaping, structural checks, dynamic mutation, temperature scheduling, and cross-policy crossover, and it uses a trace-based CRC-2 ChampSim simulator for evaluation. As an arXiv preprint, the results are not yet peer-reviewed, and the approach relies on simulation rather than silicon measurements.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Cache replacement policies decide which data to evict when a cache is full, directly affecting performance; classic policies like LRU are simple but can be suboptimal. Modern designs often use hand-crafted features or offline imitation of an optimal policy, but they struggle with dynamic workloads and complex interactions such as prefetching and thrashing. LLM-guided evolutionary search combines program synthesis with LLM reasoning to explore large design spaces, and CACHEFORGE applies this to cache replacement.

## [Language Models Predict Constraint Groups for Dantzig-Wolfe Reformulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.05726) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper proves worst-case evaluation complexity bounds for finding hidden constraint groups in Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation and shows that language models can predict such groups, verified by a staged search algorithm called JointDW. This work bridges combinatorial optimization and machine learning by using language models to guide decomposition choices, potentially speeding up mixed-integer programming solvers and reducing the need for costly column generation runs. The theoretical results show that methods observing only bounds need Θ(k^w) evaluations to find a hidden group of w families, but a prediction missing e members reduces this to Θ(k^e) via staged search; in experiments, a language model named a true group first in 249 of 252 answers for models with up to 16 families.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Dantzig-Wolfe reformulation is a technique that strengthens the linear relaxation of a mixed-integer program by convexifying constraint families, but choosing which families to convexify is hard because each candidate requires a column generation run. Column generation is an algorithm for solving large linear programs by iteratively adding variables. The paper addresses the challenge of identifying groups of constraints that only strengthen the bound when considered together.

## [Split and Bridge: Bottom-Up Multimodal Generation with Pretrained Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10441) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Split and Bridge (SnB) is a bottom-up framework that couples pretrained unimodal diffusion models at sampling time by following a shared diffusion trajectory up to a split point, then branching into modality-specific trajectories guided by a bridge module. It avoids joint training from scratch and enables plug-and-play reuse of powerful pretrained models. This approach addresses the scalability limitations of top-down multimodal methods that require joint training on large datasets, offering a more flexible and adaptable alternative. It could lower the barrier to building multimodal generative systems by leveraging existing high-quality unimodal models. SnB achieves a strong balance between sample quality and coherence on benchmarks including PolyMNIST, CelebAMask-HQ, PIE-Bench++, and ROCO, and naturally extends to zero-shot tasks such as interleaved co-generation, image editing, and style coupling/decoupling. Code is available at https://github.com/AhmadArrabi/SnB.

## [STABLE: A Primal-Dual Optimizer for Continual Learning with Adaptive Drift Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10655) ⭐️ 7.0/10

STABLE is a new primal-dual optimizer that enforces a drift budget by adaptively increasing or decreasing a dual variable, thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. The work is motivated by a formal proof showing that bounded parameter drift guarantees bounded margin erosion for distance-based classifiers under a local score-stability condition. This offers an optimizer-level alternative to standard replay buffers, architectural changes, or regularization terms, potentially providing a more general and lightweight solution to catastrophic forgetting. Experiments show that vanilla PEFT baselines trained with STABLE match or outperform specialized continual learning methods on both unimodal and CLIP-based multimodal streams, suggesting broad applicability. STABLE increases the dual variable when the drift budget is violated and decreases it otherwise, aiming for high stability without penalizing plasticity. In multimodal settings, it further preserves zero-shot transfer, matching or exceeding dedicated multimodal continual learning methods; code is available on GitHub.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Continual learning aims to train models on sequential tasks without forgetting previous knowledge, but deep neural networks suffer from catastrophic forgetting, where learning new tasks drastically degrades performance on old ones. Existing approaches typically use replay buffers, architectural changes, or regularization. The stability gap refers to the phenomenon where performance on past tasks drops significantly during learning of new data before mitigation methods recover it, highlighting the time-dependent nature of learning dynamics.

## [PURL: Joint Learning Framework for Revisable Decoding in Masked Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11551) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce PURL (Planned Unmasking-and-Revision Joint Learning), a training-based framework for masked diffusion models (MDMs) that unifies parallel generation with selective token revision. PURL derives a normalized joint transition factorized into edit selection, unmask selection, and token prediction, all trained jointly on partially masked sequences and supported by a single shared forward pass at inference. This work addresses a key limitation of independent parallel sampling in MDMs—inconsistent predictions—by enabling selective revision of early token commitments. It achieves up to 47.4% relative accuracy improvement and up to 8× reduction in decoding rounds on logic puzzles, math reasoning, and code generation, suggesting a path toward more reliable and efficient parallel text generation. PURL trains all three decision components jointly on partially masked sequences constructed according to the model's own unmasking policy, and during inference all decisions are made in a single forward pass. The analysis reveals general principles: token edits become more effective as context accumulates, early edits can steer unfinished trajectories while later edits remain localized, and effective editing depends on calibrating when to intervene and learning where and how to revise.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens in parallel, offering faster generation than autoregressive models like GPT. However, independent parallel sampling can commit to inconsistent predictions because tokens are chosen without awareness of each other. PURL builds on this paradigm by learning to selectively revise early commitments, akin to editing a draft, to improve coherence.

Researchers propose Direct Trajectory Optimization (DTO), a training-free framework that aligns text-to-image diffusion models by directly optimizing the sampling trajectory, treating intermediate denoising scores and sampled noise as optimization variables. DTO introduces Reward-Optimized Score Guidance to interpolate between optimized scores and pretrained predictions, providing a provable theoretical guarantee of reward improvement under constrained distributions. This method eliminates the need for computationally expensive backpropagation through large denoising networks, making inference-time alignment more efficient while outperforming existing methods across three diffusion models on two benchmarks. It offers a promising direction for controllable generation without retraining, which could benefit practitioners deploying diffusion models in resource-constrained settings. DTO treats intermediate denoising scores and sampled noise as optimization variables, avoiding gradients through the denoising network. The Reward-Optimized Score Guidance interpolates between optimized scores and pretrained predictions to mitigate out-of-distribution issues, and the theoretical guarantee holds under constrained distributions.

## [TopicScope: Sparse Autoencoder Features Enable Token-Level Topic Monitoring During Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12935) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduce TopicScope, a framework that trains causal topic classifiers on sparse autoencoder (SAE) features to assign a topic label to every token during generation, allowing labels to change mid-response. Monitors trained on prefill hidden states generalized to decoding across Gemma-3 1B and 4B, and remained robust to perturbations, losing at most 5 macro-F1 points. This work extends activation-based monitoring beyond binary safety classification to fine-grained, multi-class topic tracking at generation time, showing that compact monitors can be trained cheaply during prefill and deployed during decoding. It broadens the practical use of SAEs for interpretability and online guardrails in LLM applications. The team trained three detector architectures on synthetic multi-topic conversations covering seven topics; ablations showed that classifiers reaching baseline performance without SAE features were several times larger. Code, dataset, and checkpoints are released on GitHub and Hugging Face.

## [Graph Visualizations in Prompts Improve Knowledge Graph QA by 1.85 F1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12938) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A controlled study over 1,500 WebQSP and CWQ questions and six vision-language models found that adding a graph image to text prompts improves knowledge graph question answering by an average of 1.85 F1 points, with gains concentrated on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). The study also shows that multimodal gains are highly sensitive to graph layout, with hierarchical Graphviz layouts outperforming less organized renderings. This work provides actionable guidance for designing multimodal prompts in KGQA systems, showing that visual prompting can improve precision for simple queries but may hurt performance if layouts are poorly designed. It suggests adaptive policies that selectively add diagrams only for small, sparse subgraphs, which could help balance accuracy and inference efficiency in real-world deployments. The gains do not depend strongly on model scale but are highly sensitive to layout: image-only settings sharply degrade performance, and decomposing large subgraphs into separated paths yields the largest improvements. The authors argue for adaptive visual prompting that avoids unnecessary visual clutter and token overhead on complex queries.

## [SetPrint: Training-Free Black-Box LLM Fingerprinting via Setwise Response Changes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12950) ⭐️ 6.0/10

SetPrint introduces a training-free black-box LLM fingerprinting method that jointly captures within-set relations among response changes and between-set correspondence of changes induced by the same perturbation. On LeaFBench, it consistently outperforms existing training-free black-box fingerprinting methods. This work advances model provenance and attribution by improving the ability to detect whether a target model was derived from a source model using only black-box API access. Such fingerprinting is important for copyright auditing and ownership verification in the LLM ecosystem. SetPrint expresses each response change relative to the mean change of its own set, then compares changes from the two models that were induced by the same perturbation. The gains are attributed to both within-set relations and between-set correspondence, though the method is evaluated only on LeaFBench and remains a niche arXiv preprint.

## [Monitoring one channel shifts communication to shadow routes in learned agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12959) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.12959) shows that in a sender-receiver multi-agent reinforcement learning game, monitoring a visible communication channel does not eliminate communication but causes adaptive reallocation to shadow routes. Across two 20-seed batches, partial monitoring increased shadow-route share by 0.701 and 0.575 while task accuracy remained around 0.905-0.913, and frozen interventions confirmed that route information is semantic. This work has implications for AI safety and oversight of learned communication systems: simply monitoring one channel may not be sufficient to control or suppress communication, as agents can adaptively shift information to unmonitored routes. It suggests that effective oversight requires monitoring the joint message-route code rather than a single visible channel. The study uses causal interventions, including frozen message-route shuffling, which changed 0.668 of receiver predictions, and route alone retained 0.388 accuracy versus 0.25 chance. A corrected explicit-silence cost made 18/20 policies fully silent and lowered mean sending to 0.050, but the strict complete-suppression gate failed because two seeds retained communication; the authors bound the result to adaptive reallocation under partial monitoring, not open-world route discovery or emergent encryption.

The paper proposes RBLA+, a method that uses compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to extract rank-specific LoRA adapters from an aggregated global model in federated fine-tuning with heterogeneous client ranks, avoiding the formation of the dense update. It improves accuracy over its predecessor RBLA across vision and language tasks and has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline in CPU benchmarks. This work addresses a key trade-off in federated LoRA fine-tuning: direct truncation is cheap but inaccurate, while dense SVD is accurate but computationally expensive. RBLA+ offers a middle ground that preserves communication efficiency and adapter size, making heterogeneous federated fine-tuning more practical for resource-constrained clients. RBLA+ minimizes Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update, and it accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. It preserves each client's prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload, but the evaluation is limited to synthetic adapters in CPU benchmarks and specific vision/language tasks.

## [ZeroPoint: Energy-Based Model with Fixed Zero for Abstention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12992) ⭐️ 6.0/10

ZeroPoint introduces an energy-based decision model that fixes the empty answer (abstention) at zero energy for every input, providing a learned reference level to decide whether any listed option is acceptable. The model uses a small multilingual encoder that reads the input and all options jointly, and abstention is trained with the same negative log-likelihood loss as option selection. This work addresses a fundamental limitation of standard energy-based models, which only learn relative compatibility and lack a reference for deciding when no option fits. It could improve reliability in decision-making systems that need to know when to abstain, such as question answering or recommendation systems. The fixed zero energy makes the empty answer a state of the model, and options with non-negative depths measure compatibility relative to it; an option at zero depth receives no probability. Ablations show that most of the benefit comes from training with examples where no option fits, and the fixed zero separates inputs with and without an acceptable option slightly better than a learned rejection class and clearly better than a thresholded softmax.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Energy-based models (EBMs) assign a scalar energy to each joint configuration of observed and predicted variables, and inference selects the option with the lowest energy. The Gibbs distribution converts energies into probabilities, but adding a constant to all energies leaves predictions unchanged, so standard EBMs cannot decide whether any option is acceptable. ZeroPoint addresses this by anchoring the empty answer at zero energy, turning abstention into a comparison with a learned depth.

## [GRAP: Lightweight Probing Framework for Gender Bias in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13024) ⭐️ 6.0/10

GRAP introduces a lightweight logistic-probe framework that identifies the most discriminative gender-bias dimensions from rubric-scored open-ended LLM responses, moving beyond fixed-format probing tasks. It operates task-agnostically on open-ended instruction following and uses scores across 10 rubric dimensions to find which bias dimensions reliably distinguish gender groups. This matters because existing probing methods rely on fixed-format tasks that alignment-tuned models can easily handle and compare raw group-level rubric scores, ignoring per-dimension variance. GRAP addresses these limitations, offering a more nuanced way to detect subtle gender biases in open-ended LLM interactions, which is important for AI fairness and safety as LLMs increasingly mediate everyday interactions. The framework uses a logistic probe to analyze responses scored across 10 rubric dimensions, identifying the most discriminative bias dimensions without relying on fixed-format tasks. It is designed to be task-agnostic and operates on open-ended instruction following, but as an arXiv preprint, it may not yet have undergone peer review.

## [APS-VLA: Action-Guided Token Pruning Speeds Up Vision-Language-Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13030) ⭐️ 6.0/10

APS-VLA introduces a learned visual token pruning framework that keeps the pretrained VLA backbone frozen while training a lightweight Decision Influence Estimator to select a compact set of visual tokens. On two dual-arm platforms across five real-world tasks, it reduced mean inference latency from 137.25 ms to 93.25 ms (1.47× speedup) with an average success rate of 61% versus 60% for the unpruned baseline. VLA policies are increasingly used for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but processing dense visual tokens causes high inference latency that limits real-time control. APS-VLA offers a modular, plug-in optimization that preserves the underlying policy parameters and native action-generation procedure, making it applicable across different VLA architectures without retraining the backbone. The estimator is trained with two signals: action supervision that matches both full-input policy predictions and demonstrated actions, and an auxiliary visual transition objective that predicts subsequent visual features from the selected representation. At deployment, only a single hard selection and packing step is performed before the policy's native action-generation procedure, and the auxiliary predictor is removed. Experiments used OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO and π0.5 and XR-1 on RoboCasa365.

The paper introduces R2C-Agent, a decision-making agent that plans HIV prevention and treatment interventions over contact networks sampled from a new conditional graph diffusion model called Referral-to-Contact Diffusion (R2C-Diff). Simulated experiments using real-world HIV network data show that R2C-Agent empirically plans more effective interventions than baselines from interdisciplinary literature, and the paper highlights key tradeoffs and assumptions driving performance.

The paper introduces a neuro-symbolic framework that combines online-adaptive Fuzzy Cognitive Maps (FCMs) with LSTM networks for financial forecasting, featuring two variants: Framework I, which adapts FCM edges online via an error-driven Hebbian rule and uses Asymmetric Additive Residual Fusion to merge FCM and LSTM predictions, and Framework II, an LLM-augmented FCM where each edge carries a verifiable citation. Framework I uses live dual-source price series and macroeconomic indicators to construct the FCM, and its online Hebbian adaptation allows the map to converge to new market regimes within 10-15 trading days. Framework II's center-node FCMs achieved 68.9% to 85.7% state-directional accuracy, but the approach is evaluated only on NASDAQ Composite data, so generalizability to other markets or asset classes remains untested.
