## [PMR: Per-User Memory Rubrics for Personalized LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14017) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2611.14017) introduces Personalized Memory Rubrics (PMR), a framework that converts terminal QA feedback into fine-grained, per-step, per-user credit assignment for memory updates in long-horizon personalized agents. PMR uses Rubric-Guided Credit Assignment to redistribute credit at the token level, amplifying validated decisions on successful trajectories while falling back to standard policy optimization on failed ones. This addresses a key limitation in personalized agent memory: conventional training uses only terminal QA accuracy, which treats all intermediate memory updates identically and ignores that the same memory action can help one user but hurt another. PMR's per-user credit assignment could enable more effective personalization without inference overhead, benefiting developers building long-horizon assistants that must decide what to remember for each individual. PMR decomposes evaluation into a universal layer capturing cross-persona failure patterns and a per-user adaptive layer modeling individual traits as a delta over the universal baseline. The rubric and memory policy co-evolve in a closed loop with anti-circularity guarantees, and PMR incurs zero inference overhead since no rubric or external judge is needed during deployment; experiments across four benchmarks show consistent gains over strong memory-augmented baselines.

## [BARS: Budget-Aware Sequential Sampling with Refusal for Majority Identification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14171) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces BARS, a sequential sampling rule that certifies the top-two gap in an unknown distribution and can return an early stop, a budgeted majority vote, or a refusal when feasibility cannot be established. It provides a certified mode with proven error bounds and a practical mode using empirical calibration, achieving 22.3% fewer samples on GSM8K and 82.5% accuracy on MATH at the cost of refusing 18.8% and 50% of questions, respectively. This work addresses the lack of confidence estimation in early-stopping self-consistency for LLMs, enabling cost-efficient inference with statistical guarantees. It allows practitioners to make informed decisions about budget allocation and model switching, impacting deployment of LLMs in resource-constrained settings. The certified mode provides bounds on joint answering error and on refusing an instance the budget could handle, while the practical mode replaces these with empirical calibration. A refusal is a statement about the rule and its budget, not a claim that a question is unanswerable, guiding when to widen the budget or switch models.

**Background**: Self-consistency is a technique where an LLM generates multiple answers to a question and selects the most common one, improving accuracy at the cost of more computation. BARS builds on sequential analysis and the sequential probability ratio test to provide statistical guarantees for majority identification under unknown distributions.

## [Augmented Lagrangian Solver for Lifted Bellman Linear Programming in Offline RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14183) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces AL-LBLP, an augmented Lagrangian (method of multipliers) solver for Lifted Bellman Linear Programming (LBLP) in offline reinforcement learning. Unlike prior neural solver ALBUM, which uses fixed hinge penalty coefficients, AL-LBLP learns constraint multipliers via dual ascent with a single penalty parameter ρ, yielding KKT fixed points and eliminating the need for target networks. This work provides a principled optimization approach for offline RL that guarantees KKT optimality and removes the need for target networks, simplifying training. It achieves strong empirical results, including 60.1% average success on 50 OGBench tasks and 81.5% on humanoidmaze-giant, demonstrating potential for robust offline RL without unstable bootstrapping. AL-LBLP uses a single Q and V network without a target network and supports Gaussian actors, flow actors, and best-of-N sampling. It does not collapse up to batch size 8192, and for Gaussian actors, an advantage-normalized DDPG+BC objective is proposed.

**Background**: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn policies from fixed datasets without environment interaction. Traditional temporal-difference methods regress onto bootstrapped targets and often require target networks for stability. Lifted Bellman Linear Programming (LBLP) reformulates the Bellman optimality conditions as a linear program over the dataset, avoiding bootstrapping. The augmented Lagrangian method (method of multipliers) is a constrained optimization technique that combines penalty terms with Lagrange multipliers to enforce constraints, and KKT conditions are first-order necessary conditions for optimality in constrained problems.

The paper introduces RIC-TSC, a regionally-informed causal time-series classification framework that uses Joint PCMCI+ (J-PCMCI+) on multi-modal satellite and meteorological data to identify invariant predictors of supraglacial lake evolution in Greenland. On a balanced benchmark of 1000 manually labeled lakes from two contrasting melt seasons (2018-2019), causal models achieve up to 12.59% higher accuracy than correlation-based baselines under out-of-distribution evaluation. This work demonstrates that causal discovery can improve generalization under distribution shift in spatiotemporal Earth observation, moving beyond purely correlational features that often fail to transfer across heterogeneous domains. It offers a pathway to more robust and interpretable models for monitoring dynamic Earth surface processes, which is crucial for understanding ice sheet melt and sea-level rise. The framework embeds lag-aware causal discovery directly into sequence modeling, using Sentinel-1 microwave backscatter, Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8 optical reflectance, and CARRA meteorological variables. Causal graphs are estimated globally and per basin, with validated predictors and their time lags supplied to lightweight classifiers, enabling both predictive accuracy and scientific interpretability.

Distribution shift refers to changes in data distribution over time or space, which can degrade the performance of machine learning models. Causal discovery algorithms like PCMCI+ reconstruct causal graphs from time series by testing conditional independencies, and J-PCMCI+ extends this to multiple datasets with latent contexts. ## [TRAG: Textual Response-Aware Guidance Boosts Zero-Shot Adversarial Robustness of VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40309) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes Textual Response-Aware Guidance (TRAG), a method that constrains visual representation drift during adversarial fine-tuning by using the pre-trained text encoder's responses to local variations in input embeddings. It constructs anchor-level constraints from response directions and magnitudes around semantic anchors, then aggregates them using pre-trained image-anchor relevance to yield an image-adaptive constraint. This work addresses a key trade-off in adversarial fine-tuning of vision-language models: improving robustness without degrading zero-shot generalization. By preserving pre-trained image-text relationships more effectively, TRAG could enable more reliable deployment of VLMs in safety-critical applications where both robustness and zero-shot performance matter. TRAG is compared against two existing guidance forms: matching visual features (which constrains all directions equally) and matching prediction distributions (which is limited by candidate texts and prediction probabilities). Experiments across architectures and tasks show state-of-the-art clean and robust performance, and further analysis indicates TRAG helps preserve pre-trained image-text relationships.

**Background**: Vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP are trained to align images and text, enabling strong zero-shot classification. Adversarial fine-tuning is a common defense, but it often degrades the model's zero-shot generalization. ## [Möbius Interaction Filtering Regulates Higher-Order Multimodal Interactions for Humor Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12913) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes Möbius Interaction Filtering (MoIF), a method that learns a modality-subset prediction function and imposes order-selective spectral regularization through its aggregation structure. By constructing supervised unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal predictors with private temporal encoders and balanced reciprocal interaction, their uniform aggregate forms a Möbius-domain filter with geometrically decreasing interaction-order response, achieving 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1 on UR-FUNNY, exceeding thirteen reproduced methods. This work connects the organization of multimodal interactions to their statistical reliability through an executable spectral constraint, offering a novel theoretical approach for multimodal affective computing. It could improve signal-to-noise ratio in expressive fusion tasks like humor detection, where higher-order interactions often introduce noise, and the method's applicability to sentiment prediction on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI suggests broader impact. Controlled UR-FUNNY perturbations reveal a pronounced decline in label-aligned signal-to-noise ratio across interaction orders, and the induced filter improves the final ratio by 1.62-2.79 times relative to the co-trained trimodal predictor while preserving its own clean class-aligned signal under perturbation. Five-seed experiments show more stable estimates on all three datasets, and code is available at https://github.com/D-ST-Sword/MoIF.

## [Third Eye Study Questions Durability of Self-Improvement Gains in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12988) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces Third Eye, an evaluation framework that separates immediate performance gains from a model's self-update from the gains that persist after a further native update. Testing five 3-8B backbones on math and code tasks, the study finds that continuation reduces utility by 1.78 percentage points in a balanced Qwen3-4B/Llama-3.2-3B comparison, and also lowers utility for SmolLM3-3B and Llama-3.1-8B. The findings challenge the assumption that immediate gains from self-updates are a reliable proxy for the long-term value of recursive self-improvement, suggesting that evaluations should treat persistent self-updates as adaptation transitions with independent scoring and a no-update baseline. This has implications for how researchers and practitioners measure and trust self-improving LLM systems. The study uses 64 fresh runs, three candidates per run, and three continuations per candidate, with disjoint items for selection and final scoring. Candidate-averaged immediate utility is already negative, indicating that selection partly explains the apparently neutral first step, and target and out-of-distribution losses dominate retention changes, while matched recipe and recipient-donor controls identify neither a reliable mitigation nor a single mechanism.

The paper introduces structured kernel surrogate models and an SKS algorithm to measure cross-sample modality attribution, capturing how one modality in one sample affects learning outcomes in other multimodal samples. SKS uses kernel ridge regression with a compositional kernel on selection states of samples and modalities, and achieves 57.8% higher correlation with true prediction outcomes than existing methods. The paper introduces a reusable evaluation protocol to fairly compare combining frozen experts' internal features versus their final predictions, and applies it to 21 deepfake detectors from the DF40 benchmark. Under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, logistic regression on features from six architecture-diverse experts improves macro AUROC by 0.081 over the best prediction combiner. This work provides a rigorous methodology for deciding when feature-level combination outperforms prediction-level combination, which can guide ensemble design in deepfake detection and other domains where frozen experts are combined. It also highlights how evaluation choices, such as train/test overlap, can inflate apparent gains by up to 0.172 AUROC, underscoring the need for careful benchmarking. The larger feature combiner (3.5M parameters) shows no clear improvement over the linear model (10K parameters), suggesting that access to richer information matters more than combiner capacity. Weakening prediction baselines on the overlap-affected standard split inflates the apparent feature advantage, and overlap-aware evaluation changes the estimated gain.

AURA introduces a method that leverages a frozen general-audio codec, trained without spatial supervision, for spatial audio-language tasks. Through a controlled layer-wise analysis, the authors identify an audio-text information asymmetry and show that either completing the scene description or exposing inter-channel differences improves left/right accuracy, while binding directions to the queried source requires both. AURA exceeds the strongest dedicated system on SpatialSoundQA by 10.31 points in dual-source direction accuracy with only about 40% of the trainable parameters. This work challenges the prevailing need for dedicated spatial encoders in spatial audio-language models, suggesting that general audio representations can be repurposed for spatial tasks. It could simplify model architectures and reduce parameters, impacting researchers and developers working on multimodal AI, AR/VR, and audio question answering. The frozen codec retains spatial information, particularly lateral cues from inter-channel differences, but this information is not readily accessible: in dual-source scenes, a model trained on these features predicts left/right at chance and often assigns the detected direction to the wrong source. The controlled 2×2 experiment reveals that both scene description completion and inter-channel difference exposure are necessary to bind directions to the queried source.

The paper identifies a text-image mismatch in LVLM-based logical anomaly detection, where checklist decomposition is text-only and forces the model to extract different visual evidence from the same raw image, causing instance conflation and scale drift. It proposes CASCADE, a training-free framework that adds constraint-specific visual scaffolds, and CASCADE++, which adapts scaffolds at the object level; CASCADE++ surpasses the full-shot state of the art by 3.9 AUROC points on MVTec-LOCO with only three references and improves over the strongest VID-AD baseline by 11.4. This work pinpoints a fundamental perception gap in LVLM-based logical anomaly detection and shows that adapting visual input per constraint is more effective than textual reasoning guides, offering a training-free path to improve verification accuracy. It could benefit industrial inspection and quality control where logical constraints such as counts and pairings must be checked from few normal references. The method is training-free and transfers across multiple LVLM backbones without any training; the analysis compares textual reasoning guides versus visual perception guides to diagnose whether failures stem from insufficient reasoning or perception. CASCADE++ derives scaffold configurations from constraint structure and reference distribution at the object level, and evaluations are on MVTec-LOCO and VID-AD benchmarks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Logical Anomaly Detection (LAD) requires verifying whether category-specific constraints such as object counts, pairing relations, and measurement ranges are satisfied by a query image given only a few normal references. Recent LAD methods based on Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) formulate this as checklist verification, decomposing the decision into independent textual checks. LVLMs are multimodal systems that combine vision encoders with large language models to perform tasks such as visual question answering and image captioning. This paper shows that the text-only decomposition creates a constraint-specific perception gap, because every checklist item reads the same unmodified query image.

## [PolyRoute: A 12-Language Benchmark for Typed-Decision Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13843) ⭐️ 6.0/10

PolyRoute introduces a benchmark of 322 native-language support messages across 12 languages and 9 writing systems, plus 156 code-mixed or romanised messages (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi), for a three-way department-routing decision. It includes baselines and a leaderboard comparing 13 systems, with the best fine-tune reaching 96.6% accuracy and TF-IDF with logistic regression reaching 91.9%. Typed-decision encoders are increasingly used for routing tasks, but their behavior outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. PolyRoute provides a multilingual and code-mixed evaluation resource that can reveal performance gaps and guide model selection for non-English routing applications. Labels were generated by Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept), and an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items; the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test and training text is 0.33. The split only resolves differences above about 4 points, and on code-mixed text the English-root checkpoint (85%) nominally outperforms the shipped multilingual checkpoint (79%; p=0.134).

## [MicroBT: Centroid-Guided Learning for Micro Brain Tumor Segmentation and Counting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13912) ⭐️ 6.0/10

MicroBT introduces a centroid-anchored synergistic paradigm that uses predicted lesion centroids as shared anchors to jointly condition dense segmentation and instance-level localization, addressing scale bias against sub-3mm micro-lesions. It also proposes a Volume-Calibrated Loss (VC-Loss) and Size-Aware Curriculum Optimization (SACO), achieving ~7% improvement in micro-lesion localization precision and ~26% reduction in counting errors on brain metastases. This work tackles a clinically critical limitation: standard overlap-based segmentation objectives systematically suppress small lesions, which can affect cancer staging and treatment planning. By unifying segmentation and counting with scale-invariant centroid anchors, MicroBT offers a more reliable tool for detecting and quantifying micro-metastases, potentially improving clinical decision-making for brain tumor patients. The framework builds on nnU-Net v2 and adds the Centroid-Anchored Synergy (CAS) module, VC-Loss, and a two-stage SACO training strategy. While it achieves state-of-the-art results with comparable computational cost, the evaluation focuses on brain metastases and may require validation on broader tumor types and multi-center datasets.

## [TIGA: Tool-Grounded LLM Agents for Controlled Taxonomy Induction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13966) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduced TIGA (Taxonomy Induction with Tool-Grounded Agents), a knowledge-engineering architecture that formulates taxonomy induction as an iterative decision process over an explicit state and constrained action space. TIGA combines executable taxonomy-editing tools, an interaction memory recording tool calls, rationales, and outcomes, and a runtime-adaptive organizational policy that the agent revises during inference, with an optional global reviewer. Automated taxonomy construction is labor-intensive and error-prone, and LLM free-form generation often produces omitted or hallucinated entities and invalid hierarchical relations. TIGA's tool-grounded, policy-driven approach offers a more controlled way to build complete, structurally valid, and semantically coherent hierarchies, which could benefit semantic search, recommendation, product catalogs, and retrieval-augmented generation. Evaluated on four benchmark taxonomies with two LLM backbones, TIGA achieved the strongest structural-quality results in most configurations but did not dominate every precision measure, and gains came with substantially higher token consumption, API-call volume, and inference time. Ablations show consistent benefits from the policy and interaction-memory components, while the effect of global review depends on the dataset and revision budget.

## [Model-Free Runtime Monitor Detects Stalled Information Acquisition in Autonomous Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14111) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Acquisition-State Telemetry (AST), a model-free architecture that monitors whether an autonomous system's ongoing information gathering is progressing toward declared task requirements. AST maps raw observations into task-resolution coordinates and emits two continuous real-time signals: prospective progress across unresolved requirements and informational friction when recurrent evidence yields negligible gain. Autonomous systems can remain operationally active without resolving outstanding mission requirements, and AST fills a gap by monitoring the live process of information gathering rather than just outcomes. This could improve reliability in search and rescue, robotic manipulation, and reinforcement learning agents by detecting unproductive stagnation early. A single, unadjusted monitor configuration was evaluated across eight diverse domains, including search and rescue dialogue, spatial grid exploration, hierarchical capability acquisition, continuous robotic manipulation, and probabilistic intent estimation. In closed-loop reinforcement learning experiments with early termination constraints, penalizing informational friction allowed agents to sustain high mission success, whereas unpenalized policies and baselines with matched operational costs failed to complete required tasks.

The approach is model-free, meaning it does not rely on a learned model of the environment or task.

A reanalysis of trial-level data from Lewis & Frank (2018) found that the DINOv2 distance between test images and teaching examples predicted adults' word extension (log odds -3.23 per SD, N=520), and example composition strongly influenced generalization (1.1% superordinate extension after subordinate examples vs. 77.5% after superordinate examples). An artificial learner using the same encoder also showed lower naming accuracy for word pairs spanning more distant categories (84.7%, 65.4%, and 53.0% for near, mid, and far pairs). This work bridges cognitive science and self-supervised computer vision by showing that a frozen DINOv2 encoder captures part of the visual similarity structure underlying human word generalization, suggesting that such models can serve as quantitative tools for studying semantic development. It also highlights that teaching example composition contributes information beyond visual distance, which matters for designing effective word-learning interventions and for building more cognitively plausible AI learners. The encoder's distances correlated with human similarity and confusability measures from three datasets (rho = .501–.795), but this alignment did not conclusively show that human-derived distances predict learner difficulty, and a second encoder trained on one child's experience reproduced the tier ordering but not the pair-level effect. ## [VATC: A Verifiable QoS Class for LLM-Agent Traffic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14211) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper proposes the Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class (VATC), which uses a reserved DSCP value to declare agent traffic, a router-side classifier that demotes non-compliant flows to a class served after best-effort traffic, and a rate-limited priority queue. It was evaluated in two simulators and on a real Linux kernel, showing a 98% reduction in mean agent queuing delay versus DiffServ in a constructed burst (at a 12% increase in human delay) and holding human latency 11 times below DiffServ under a spoofed flood. As LLM-based software agents generate traffic patterns distinct from human web traffic, routers currently lack a dedicated class and cannot verify a sender's claim to be an agent. VATC addresses this gap by combining marking, verification, and policing, which could influence future QoS standards and router implementations for agentic AI workloads. VATC matched DiffServ under steady load, but without verification, DiffServ and a tightly configured fq_codel gave legitimate agents lower latency than VATC. A live four-feature classifier demoted all 20 bulk-shaped spoofers but missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern, and with emulated network delay a timing feature stopped separating agent from human flows; the traffic was synthetic or sandbox-scale.

A new arXiv paper proposes design criteria for generating synthetic training data that enable neural network channel estimators to generalize across diverse wireless channels with varying Doppler shifts and power delay profiles. ## [Branch-and-Bound vs. A* for Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14426) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper compares Branch-and-Bound (B&B) and A* search for the Resource-Constrained Project Scheduling Problem (RCPSP), establishing relationships between mixed-integer linear programming, state-action, and timed Petri-net representations. Experiments on 480 benchmark instances show that graph-based A* substantially outperforms the B&B variants, proving optimality for all 480 instances versus 445 for best-first B&B under the same time and memory limits. This work clarifies the computational trade-offs between two major exact search paradigms from Operations Research and AI, highlighting the importance of duplicate-state detection and offering guidance for researchers to select appropriate methods or incorporate effective mechanisms from one approach into the other. It has implications for solving NP-hard scheduling problems more efficiently. The study uses relatively basic implementations with the same lower bound and best-first node selection to isolate the effects of search mechanisms, particularly the identification of equivalent states reached through different scheduling decision sequences. Depth-first B&B uses less memory and can find feasible solutions even when the search does not finish within the time limit, while stronger linear programming relaxations reduce the search space but introduce considerable computational overhead.

The paper establishes that the do-calculus is both sound and complete for identifying macro causal effects in cluster-directed mixed graphs (C-DMGs) over acyclic directed mixed graphs (ADMGs) when cluster sizes are unknown or greater than one. This work addresses a real gap in causal inference by handling partially specified causal systems, which are common in medicine and epidemiology where complete causal knowledge is unavailable. The paper introduces Market Regime Council (MRC), an online Shapley-based credit-assignment mechanism for multi-agent LLM portfolio management that stabilizes early periods via a Bayesian adaptive mixture and adjusts agent authority with regime-dependent multipliers. Over 1,037 trading days across 13 crypto assets and five seeds, MRC achieved a Sharpe ratio of 1.51 and a cumulative return of 440.1%, ranking first on cumulative return, Sharpe ratio, and information ratio among active baselines while attaining the lowest maximum drawdown. This work addresses a core challenge in multi-agent LLM systems—fairly assigning credit among specialist agents—and demonstrates that Shapley-weighted coalition integration can improve financial decision-making. The approach could inform credit-assignment designs in other multi-agent LLM applications where transparency and robustness to regime shifts are critical. MRC computes exact Shapley credits across all single, pairwise, and Grand-coalition outputs for N=3 specialist agents, recomputing weights each trading period from exponentially weighted performance histories and recording each rebalance through a five-layer causal trace. Ablation results show that gains stem from Shapley-weighted integration across coalition outputs rather than any single stage in isolation, and code and demo data are open source.

## [OHCAM learns conditional and quantified action models via uncertainty-guided exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.30955) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers present Online Hypothesis-Driven Conditional Action Model Learning (OHCAM), an online method that learns action models with conditional and quantified effects from limited, noisy interactions by maintaining a belief over hypotheses and selecting actions that maximize disagreement among them. OHCAM starts with simple hypotheses and expands to more complex conditions only when current hypotheses become inconsistent with data, and it was validated on six benchmark planning domains plus two tasks with a Kinova Gen3 robot. Accurate action models are essential for effective planning, yet prior methods either assume simple action representations or become computationally intractable when handling conditional and quantified effects. OHCAM's sample-efficient, noise-robust online learning could make planning more practical in real-world robotics settings where interactions are costly and observations are imperfect. The method uses disagreement among competing hypotheses as an active-learning signal to reduce uncertainty, and it explicitly handles observation noise. Experiments show it learns models that solve substantially more tasks than baselines on six benchmark domains, though the evaluation is limited to those domains and two robot tasks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Action-model learning is the problem of inferring the preconditions and effects of actions so that an AI planner can reason about what will happen when an action is executed. Conditional effects mean an action's outcome depends on the state (e.g., moving an object only if it is not locked), while quantified effects involve applying an effect to all objects satisfying some condition. Active learning selects the most informative queries or actions to label or try, and disagreement-based exploration uses the variance among an ensemble of hypotheses to decide where to explore next.

## [FAIDER: Fairness-Aware Item-Level Decoding for LLM Recommenders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10285) ⭐️ 6.0/10

FAIDER introduces a decoding-time fairness method for LLM-based recommenders that selects complete item candidates rather than manipulating token-level logits, using conformal-inspired calibration to set a cross-group semantic-disparity threshold and online decoding with hard filtering or a soft penalty to target a prescribed violation rate. The authors prove that under a uniform enforceability assumption, the soft decoder's empirical violation rate exceeds its target by at most O(1/T), and experiments show Soft FAIDER improves both semantic fairness and ranking quality over prompt-repair baselines. This work addresses fairness in LLM recommenders when model weights and full-vocabulary logits are inaccessible, a realistic black-box setting for many deployed systems. It offers a theoretically grounded, decoding-time alternative to prompt repair, which could help practitioners control cross-group recommendation disparities without retraining or model access. FAIDER separates the operational criterion for a violation from the strength of generation constraint, using conformal-inspired empirical calibration for the threshold and dual-inspired feedback to adjust the soft penalty online. The pathwise guarantee depends on a uniform enforceability assumption, and results indicate that stricter per-recommendation constraints (hard filtering) do not necessarily yield lower measured disparity than the soft variant.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: LLM-based recommenders generate item suggestions as text, and prior work shows that changing a user's protected attribute (e.g., gender or race) can alter recommendations even with identical interaction history. Conformal prediction is a statistical framework for uncertainty quantification that produces valid prediction sets under exchangeability assumptions, and here it inspires calibration of a fairness threshold. Decoding-time interventions modify the generation process itself, which is attractive when model internals are hidden, but item-level selection differs from token-level logit manipulation because recommendations are complete items rather than independent tokens.

## [Graph Energy Matching: Transport-Aligned Energy-Based Modeling for Graph Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.23398) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Graph Energy Matching (GEM) is a new discrete energy-based generative framework for graph generation that learns a permutation-invariant potential energy to guide transport from noise to high-likelihood graph regions, inspired by the Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) transport-map optimization perspective. It introduces an energy-based switching sampling protocol that bridges rapid gradient-guided transport and local mixing, and on molecular graph benchmarks it matches or surpasses strong discrete diffusion baselines on most reported metrics. Discrete energy-based models have historically lagged behind discrete diffusion models in sample fidelity due to spurious local minima and training instability, so GEM's ability to close this gap while retaining composable, constraint-aware inference could make EBMs a more practical choice for molecular discovery and materials design. Its relative likelihood modeling also enables targeted exploration such as compositional generation, property-constrained sampling, and interpolation between graphs. GEM addresses off-support regions that trap samplers by learning a permutation-invariant potential energy that both guides discrete transport toward high-likelihood regions and refines samples within them, with a switching strategy that alternates between gradient-guided transport and local mixing. The abstract reports matching or surpassing discrete diffusion baselines on most metrics, but does not specify the exact benchmark datasets or the magnitude of improvements.

**Background**: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a probability distribution through an unnormalized potential energy function, which makes them attractive for composable inference and constraint enforcement but notoriously difficult to sample from in discrete spaces. Discrete diffusion models such as DiGress have become a strong baseline for graph generation by progressively adding and removing edges and changing node categories through a noising process. The Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) scheme is a time-discretization procedure that iteratively solves optimization problems involving the Wasserstein distance between probability measures, and GEM draws on this transport-map perspective to align its sampling with a gradient flow toward high-likelihood regions.

COMO introduces Minimum Risk Training (MRT) to optical chemical structure recognition (OCSR), directly optimizing molecule-level non-differentiable objectives like chemical validity and structural similarity to mitigate exposure bias. Experiments on ten benchmarks show it outperforms rule-based and learning-based methods with less training data, and ablation studies confirm MRT is architecture-agnostic. This work addresses a key limitation of token-level maximum likelihood training in OCSR, potentially improving accuracy on real-world chemical diagrams from patents and literature. COMO optimizes directly over molecule-level criteria such as chemical validity and structural similarity, which are non-differentiable, and achieves superior performance across ten benchmarks including synthetic and real-world diagrams. ## [Adaptive Reparameterized Time Learns Diffusion Sampling Schedules via RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.02137) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change for score-based diffusion sampling by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control. It also proposes ART-RL, a randomized reinforcement learning formulation with Gaussian policies that solves the deterministic control problem and is proven equivalent to ART at the optimizer level. This work offers a principled, plug-and-play method to improve sample quality of existing diffusion samplers by only changing the timestep grid, which could benefit a wide range of generative modeling applications without retraining the model. The learned schedules also generalize across budgets, datasets, solvers, and pipelines, making them practical for deployment. ART is based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate that provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. The ART-RL formulation uses Gaussian policies and actor-critic updates derived from trajectory-based moment identities, and experiments show consistent improvement over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets.

## [SplitLite Cuts Split-Learning Communication via Low-Rank Residual Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23018) ⭐️ 6.0/10

SplitLite, a new method for communication-efficient split federated LoRA fine-tuning of on-device LLMs, exploits the low effective rank of activation and gradient residuals between consecutive epochs. By transmitting only quantized truncated SVD residual factors, it reduces activation uplink traffic by up to 93.5% and total communication by up to 88.6% on GLUE benchmarks without hurting model performance. Communication overhead is a major bottleneck for split learning on resource-constrained devices, so cutting it by nearly an order of magnitude could make federated LoRA fine-tuning of on-device LLMs far more practical. The work is relevant to both the federated learning and on-device LLM communities, though it remains an incremental optimization rather than a paradigm shift. The key finding is that with the pretrained backbone frozen and LoRA updates being low-rank, the activation and gradient residuals of the same sample across adjacent epochs concentrate most of their energy in a few singular directions. SplitLite therefore sends quantized truncated SVD factors of these residuals, targeting both activation uplink and gradient downlink traffic; results are reported on the GLUE benchmark across several advanced on-device LLMs.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Federated learning trains models across distributed clients without sharing raw data, while split learning instead splits a model between client and server, offloading most computation to the server. Split federated learning combines both, and LoRA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that freezes pretrained weights and trains small low-rank adapter matrices. In split learning, however, clients and server must exchange high-dimensional activations and gradients every round, which becomes a prohibitive communication cost for large models.

SCFT combines local spectral convolution, permutation-equivariant beam-set attention, and a query-based Transformer decoder to detect and classify line-of-sight and non-line-of-sight paths. The evaluation uses realistic ray-tracing data, and the method is benchmarked against ResNet as the strongest competing baseline.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: In mmWave and 6G systems, wireless signals travel along multiple paths (multipath components) between transmitter and receiver, each characterized by delay, AoA, and AoD. These geometric parameters are crucial for tasks like positioning and radio SLAM, which uses radio signals for simultaneous localization and mapping. Traditional learning-based channel estimators focus on communication objectives rather than explicitly estimating these parameters, motivating the proposed approach.

## [LLM Repair Agent Uses Learned Router for Selective External Evidence Retrieval in Knowledge Graph Repair](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07342) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces a framework for selective retrieval in iterative knowledge graph repair, where an LLM repair agent edits the graph while a trained router decides when to query an external researcher agent for evidence. It extends a violation-injection framework to generate cases with multiple compatible violations and known reference repairs, using the agent's repair outcomes as supervision to train a deployment-specific router. This work addresses the costly and unreliable nature of external evidence retrieval in graph repair by learning when retrieval is beneficial, which could improve repair accuracy while reducing token usage. It is relevant to practitioners building LLM-agent systems for data quality and knowledge graph maintenance. On two building-automation datasets, researcher access improved repairs for some violations but degraded them for others, with effects varying across deployments. The router used fewer repair-time tokens than always enabling access in all six evaluation suites and achieved higher repair F1 than always disabling access in five of six suites.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Knowledge graphs often contain missing or inconsistent facts that undermine downstream applications. Schema validation can detect violations but does not indicate which of several valid repairs recovers the intended graph, and external corpora that could supply evidence are costly to query. Violation-injection frameworks generate test cases by deliberately introducing violations with known repairs, providing supervision for repair methods.

## [CLEAR-WSI: Scalable Diagnostic-Driven Retrieval for Pathology Archives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07935) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers present CLEAR-WSI, a scalable, diagnostic-driven framework for content-based retrieval of whole-slide pathology images using fixed-length slide embeddings. Validated on two public and one private clinical dataset across four retrieval tasks, it improves Precision@5 over the strongest baseline by 3.10 on CAMELYON16, 2.75 on BRACS-1, 1.95 on BRACS-2, and 3.75 on X-HER2. Digital pathology archives are growing rapidly, but inconsistent or missing metadata makes navigation difficult; content-based retrieval can help pathologists find similar cases directly from images. CLEAR-WSI's fixed-length embedding and expanding memory bank offer a scalable approach that could support clinical decision support and case-based learning in real-world pathology workflows. CLEAR-WSI refines retrieved candidates using either a predicted diagnostic label or the ground-truth label, depending on the retrieval setting, and adds newly processed cases to an expanding memory bank. The study includes ablation and latency analyses, though the private clinical dataset and full deployment details are not publicly disclosed.

However, existing pathology retrieval systems often rely on handcrafted indexing pipelines and predefined sampling strategies, limiting scalability and generalization.

## [BEiTScore++ adds calibrated confidence intervals to image captioning evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09505) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers propose BEiTScore++, an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric that uses conformalized quantile regression to produce calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. The method models predictive distributions over human judgments in a single forward pass and is evaluated on multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings. Reliable uncertainty estimation is crucial for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings where input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. BEiTScore++ enables practitioners to know when to trust an image-caption alignment score, which could improve the reliability of automatic evaluation in vision-language research and applications. BEiTScore++ preserves the ranking correlation of the original BEiTScore while producing intervals whose width tracks prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, demonstrating sensitivity to distribution shift.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: BEiTScore is a reference-free image captioning evaluation metric built on the BEiT-3 multimodal foundation model, which uses Multiway Transformers for unified vision and vision-language pretraining. Conformalized quantile regression combines conformal prediction with quantile regression to construct prediction intervals with valid coverage guarantees. This work extends BEiTScore by adding such calibrated intervals for uncertainty-aware evaluation.

## [CulturalCrosswords: A 42-Language Benchmark for LLM Crossword Solving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10044) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduced CulturalCrosswords, a benchmark of 53 crosswords built from crowdsourced cultural riddles in 42 languages, and evaluated 11 LLM configurations on five clue-set variants. On 962 clues with alternative answers, providing answer lengths improved agreement with the reference by 22.8 percentage points, versus 8.4 points when accepted alternatives also received credit. This work highlights a flaw in exact-match scoring for culturally grounded riddles, where multiple valid answers exist, and shows that answer constraints and grid completion reveal model differences that simple accuracy hides. It offers a more nuanced evaluation method for multilingual and cultural knowledge in LLMs. The benchmark distinguishes agreement with a reference from the ability to produce answers that fit together and occupy correct cells; crossword input increased the share of compatible crossings by 9.7 points, and requiring a completed grid exposed large differences between models. The study used 11 LLM configurations and five versions of each clue set, including plain batches, batches with lengths, batches with lengths and partial-answer hints, and crosswords requesting an answer list or a completed grid.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: Exact-match scoring is a common evaluation metric that checks whether a model's output exactly matches a reference answer, but it can penalize valid alternative answers. Crossword puzzles are constraint satisfaction problems where answers must satisfy both clue semantics and grid constraints such as length and crossing letters. Cultural riddles draw on community-specific knowledge, making them a challenging test of LLM cultural understanding.

## [Transferred-angle QAOA on superconducting hardware retains little probability of optimum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10529) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2611.10529v2) reports experiments on IBM's Heron processor ibm_marrakesh using depth-2 transferred-angle QAOA circuits for binary subproblems of an alternating-direction decomposition. At 12 qubits, the circuits retained 29%–46% of their mean-gap improvement but only 5%–15% of their probability of the optimum, showing that mean-gap metrics can mask severe loss of optimal bitstrings. This finding cautions against using mean gap alone to validate QAOA hardware performance, as it can overstate the device's ability to find optimal solutions. It suggests that practitioners should report retention of the optimum and near-optimal sets to accurately assess optimization quality on quantum processors. The study used dynamical decoupling and twirling, and found that near-optimal bitstrings were lost about as much as the optimum, while avoidance of poor bitstrings was retained best. A device-matched noise model overestimated the retention of the optimum five- to eightfold, and on a rugged planted family the device found the optimum in 62% of 768-shot blocks versus 98% noiseless.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Nov 11, 05:00

**Background**: QAOA is a variational quantum algorithm for combinatorial optimization, where parameterized circuits are executed on quantum hardware. Transferred-angle QAOA uses parameters trained on one problem instance for another, exploiting parameter concentration. IBM Heron is a 156-qubit superconducting processor, and dynamical decoupling and twirling are error mitigation techniques used to suppress decoherence and coherent errors.
